query: Equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr exhibits 8–16% room-temperature tensile ductility in the cast state and a yield strength of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C at strain rates of 10−4–10−2 s−1, but inadequate oxygen resistance prevents most practical high-temperature applications. Earlier oxidation-protection research prevented pesting in a related, non-equiatomic Hf–Nb–Ta–Ti–Zr alloy during a 5 h exposure to air at 800 °C, but that result does not establish protection for equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr; related studies on other refractory alloys likewise did not evaluate this composition. With preservation of useful room- and high-temperature mechanical performance as a design constraint, what single intervention could improve the oxygen resistance of equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr? Formulate one hypothesis identifying the intervention and mechanism, predicting the outcome relative to untreated material, defining the applicable temperature, atmosphere, exposure-time, and loading boundaries, citing supporting evidence from the prior studies, and specifying a controlled experiment and result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Introduce a designed trace reactive‐element microalloying addition by incorporating ~0.5 at.% yttrium (Y) into equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr with supporting thermodynamic assessments to ensure that Y remains in solid solution and preferentially segregates to oxide–metal interfaces during oxidation.
generation.material_initial_state: Equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr produced by conventional arc melting with a homogeneous bcc matrix and known inadequate oxygen resistance (pesting) at 800–1200 °C.
generation.intervention: Add ~0.5 at.% Y during alloy melting. Prior to full-scale experiments, perform CALPHAD or similar thermodynamic modeling to confirm that Y does not form deleterious bulk phases at this concentration and is predicted to segregate to grain boundaries and near-surface regions during subsequent thermal exposures.
generation.conditions: Casting by arc melting in argon (using high‐purity elements), followed by standard heat treatment. Oxidation tests in air at 800 °C and 1200 °C for up to 5 hours; mechanical (tensile) tests at room temperature and at 1000 °C at strain rates between 10^–4 and 10^–2 s^–1.
generation.structural_mediator: Localized enrichment of Y at the oxide scale/metal interface and grain boundaries without perturbing the overall microstructure.
generation.mechanism: Y has a high oxygen affinity and is well known to produce the ‘reactive element effect’ in high‐temperature alloys. In this system, Y is expected to segregate at interfaces, reduce the mobility of the oxide–metal boundary, and inhibit the formation of voids and pores. This improves the adhesion and continuity of the protective oxide layer. Thermodynamic guidance ensures that the Y addition is low enough to avoid formation of brittle Y‐rich phases that would otherwise compromise mechanical properties.
generation.predicted_outcome: The Y-doped alloy should show a lower overall oxidation weight gain, diminished oxide scale spallation, and more continuous, adherent oxide scales compared with the undoped baseline, while retaining similar room- and high-temperature tensile ductility and yield strength. The expected improvement is qualitatively significant though precise quantitative gains remain uncertain.
generation.baseline: Untreated equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr without any reactive element microalloying.
generation.boundary: The beneficial effect is anticipated as long as Y is maintained at ~0.5–1 at.% (to prevent second phase precipitation) and is validated for oxidation exposures up to 5 hours in the 800–1200 °C range.
generation.uncertainty: The precise segregation behavior of Y and its impact on oxide scale chemistry in this five-element refractory system is not fully quantified; thermodynamic modeling offers guidance, but experimental validation is required.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples – one with ~0.5 at.% Y and one without. Use surface-sensitive techniques (e.g., XPS, TEM-EDS) to verify Y segregation at the oxide scale and grain boundaries after controlled heat treatments. Conduct isothermal oxidation tests in air at 800 °C and 1200 °C for 5 hours, measuring oxidation mass gains and oxide scale morphology via SEM and XRD. In parallel, perform tensile tests at room temperature and 1000 °C.
measurements: Y concentration profiles at/near the oxide scale
Oxidation mass gain and detailed scale morphology (spallation, continuity)
Tensile yield strength and ductility at room and high temperature
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Y-doped alloy does not exhibit significant Y enrichment at the desired interfaces or fails to show measurable improvements in oxide scale adherence and reduced oxidation mass gain—without a detrimental change in mechanical properties relative to the undoped control—the hypothesis is falsified.

The two major types of austenitic stainless steels are characterized by the oxide layer that forms on the steel surface: either chromia-forming or alumina-forming. Cr-forming stainless steel is the most common type. However, Cr-forming steels do not exhibit high creep resistance at high temperatures, especially in environments with water vapor. Exposure to water vapor at high temperatures can increase internal oxidation in Cr-forming alloys and rapid formation of volatile Cr (oxy)hydroxides, both of which can reduce durability and lifetime. Al-forming austenitic stainless steels feature a single-phase matrix of austenite iron (FCC) with an Al-oxide at the surface of the steel. Al is more thermodynamically stable in oxygen than Cr. More commonly, however, precipitate phases are introduced to increase strength and creep resistance. In Al-forming steels, NiAl precipitates are introduced to act as Al reservoirs to maintain the protective alumina layer. In addition, Nb and Cr additions help form and stabilize Al by increasing precipitate volume fractions of NiAl. paper_did: Fabricated and characterized a novel RHEA (NV1) with elements Al, Cr, Mo, Nb, Si, Ta, and Ti using cold crucible levitation melting and standard machining.
Conducted long‐term isothermal oxidation experiments in air at 1000 °C and 1100 °C for up to 200 hours, measuring mass gain with thermogravimetric analysis.
Performed comprehensive phase and microstructure analyses (XRD, SEM/EDS, TEM) to identify the nature of the oxide scales, internal oxidation, and nitridation zones.
paper_reported: At 1000 °C, NV1 exhibited an exponential mass gain (6.53 mg/cm² after 200 hours) with a porous, externally formed CrTaO4‐based oxide containing dispersed Al2O3 and Cr2O3.

At 1100 °C, the alloy’s mass gain was lower (4.03 mg/cm²) and the oxidation kinetics followed three distinct stages, associated with the formation of a denser, protective CrTaO4-based scale and the development of internal oxidation and nitridation regions.

The as-cast dendritic microstructure produced compositional heterogeneities that led to nonuniform oxidation, and the role of reactive elements (e.g., Si) and CrTaO4 non‐stoichiometry were highlighted as important factors in oxidation resistance.
paper_proposed: Further investigations into the oxidation mechanism of NV1, especially the detailed role and evolution of the CrTaO4‐based oxide, are suggested.
Exploration of the impact of additional alloying elements (such as Si) and the influence of nitridation on the long‐term oxidation behavior is recommended.
Studies to determine whether alternate processing routes or compositional adjustments can promote the formation of more protective (continuous and denser) oxide scales are proposed.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Introduce a minor aluminum addition (e.g. 3–5 at%) to equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr to promote the in situ formation of a continuous, slow-growing Al2O3 scale that passivates the surface against oxygen ingress.
hypotheses.material_initial_state: Equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr as cast, exhibiting a dendritic microstructure with near–equal elemental distribution.
hypotheses.intervention: Alloy composition modification by substituting a few atomic percent of one element (for instance, a partial reduction in Hf content) with Al.
hypotheses.conditions: Oxidation testing in air at 1000–1100 °C for exposures up to 200 hours; mechanical characterization at room temperature and high temperatures to verify ductility and yield strength preservation.
hypotheses.structural_mediator: The formation of a dense, adherent Al2O3 scale on the alloy’s surface.
hypotheses.mechanism: Aluminum has a high affinity for oxygen, and even a minor addition can lead to the rapid formation of a thermodynamically stable, slow-growing oxide layer (Al2O3) which is known to provide effective barrier properties. This layer minimizes both inward oxygen diffusion and outward metal cation migration, thereby enhancing oxidation resistance without a detrimental impact on the room- and high-temperature mechanical properties.
hypotheses.predicted_outcome: A substantial reduction in oxidation weight gain relative to the untreated equiatomic alloy – likely shifting from rapid (exponential) mass gain towards a parabolic or even near-protective regime – while preserving the tensile ductility and yield strength ranges.
hypotheses.baseline: Untreated equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr that suffers from inadequate oxidation resistance under similar test conditions.
hypotheses.boundary: The intervention is expected to be effective between 1000 and 1100 °C and should be verified for exposure durations up to 200 hours in air.
hypotheses.uncertainty: The precise amount of Al that preserves mechanical performance while ensuring an effective continuous oxide scale needs optimization.

hypotheses.builds_on: The paper’s finding that formation of a protective external oxide (e.g., CrTaO4-based in NV1) can slow oxidation, paired with established superalloy principles where Al additions form protective Al2O3 layers.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Introduce a small silicon addition (e.g. ~1–2 at%) into equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr to encourage the formation of Si-enriched oxide or silicate phases that reduce oxygen penetration and also help mitigate nitridation.
hypotheses.material_initial_state: Equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr with its original dendritic, heterogeneous cast microstructure lacking silicon.
hypotheses.intervention: Minor alloying element modification by adding approximately 1–2 at% Si, potentially by partially substituting another element (e.g. a slight reduction in Ta or Ti content) while maintaining overall equiatomic balance.
hypotheses.conditions: Exposure in air at 1100 °C for 200 hours with subsequent assessment of oxidation resistance, and mechanical performance tests at room temperature and elevated temperatures.
hypotheses.structural_mediator: The formation of a thin, adherent silicate-modified oxide scale (or incorporation of Si into the existing oxide phases) on the alloy surface.
hypotheses.mechanism: Silicon can segregate to the oxide scale during high-temperature exposure and promote the formation of silicate phases that are typically more dense and less permeable to oxygen. In addition, as indicated in the paper (e.g. discussions around Si’s role in nitridation resistance in NV1), Si additions reduce the ingress of nitrogen, further stabilizing the scale. The net result is a barrier layer that reduces both oxygen and nitrogen diffusion without markedly altering the bulk mechanical properties.
hypotheses.predicted_outcome: A noticeable reduction in oxidation mass gain (improved parabolic behavior) at 1100 °C and improved resistance to nitridation, while retaining mechanical properties comparable to the untreated alloy. The protective scale should be leaner in defects.
hypotheses.baseline: The untreated equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr alloy that shows inadequate oxygen resistance and possible heterogeneous oxidation-induced defects.
hypotheses.boundary: This intervention is considered for oxidation conditions at approximately 1100 °C and long-term exposures (up to 200 hours) in air.
hypotheses.uncertainty: The exact impact on mechanical performance after minor Si addition is not fully established and may require fine-tuning to avoid embrittlement.

hypotheses.material_initial_state: As-cast equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr with a dendritic microstructure that exhibits compositional heterogeneity leading to heterogeneous oxidation behavior.
hypotheses.intervention: Apply a homogenization heat treatment to the as-cast alloy at 1200–1300 °C for an optimized duration (e.g. several hours) to reduce chemical segregation and improve microstructural uniformity.
hypotheses.conditions: Post-treatment oxidation testing in air at 1000–1100 °C over 200 hours, along with mechanical testing at room temperature (tensile ductility) and at high temperature (yield strength).
hypotheses.structural_mediator: A more uniform and refined microstructure with reduced chemical segregation, leading to a homogeneous, continuous, and less porous oxide scale formation during oxidation.
hypotheses.mechanism: In the as-cast state, the dendritic microstructure promotes heterogeneous oxidation due to locally varying compositions, as observed in the paper. A homogenization heat treatment can eliminate or significantly diminish these compositional gradients. This enhanced uniformity facilitates more even diffusion of alloying elements during oxidation, promoting the formation of an oxide layer with fewer defects and gaps. A denser, coherent oxide scale reduces oxygen ingress, thereby improving oxidation resistance while minimally affecting the intrinsic mechanical properties.
hypotheses.predicted_outcome: A reduction in the oxidation rate (lower mass gain) and a more uniform oxide scale as evidenced by cross-sectional microstructural analysis. Mechanical property testing should show retention of ductility (8–16% at room temperature) and yield strength (163–530 MPa at 1000 °C) comparable to the untreated alloy.
hypotheses.baseline: The as-cast equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr alloy with its dendritic microstructure and non-uniform oxidation behavior.
hypotheses.boundary: This process is applicable for alloys intended for oxidation conditions in air at 1000–1100 °C with exposures up to 200 hours, provided that the heat treatment does not induce grain growth that could adversely affect mechanical properties.
hypotheses.uncertainty: The optimal heat treatment temperature and duration must be balanced to achieve homogenization without excessive grain growth, and the effect on oxidation resistance is predicted qualitatively.

paper_did: Fabricated a series of refractory high‐entropy alloys using the subtraction method – starting with equiatomic HfMoNbTaTiZr and then removing one element at a time (e.g. HfNbTaTiZr, HfMoTaTiZr, HfMoNbTiZr, HfMoNbTaZr, HfMoNbTaTi) by vacuum‐arc melting with multiple re‐melting steps for chemical homogeneity.

Characterized the microstructure and phase using BSE imaging, SEM-EDS, and X‐ray diffraction, confirming the formation of a single-phase BCC disordered solid solution with dendritic structures and elemental segregation.

Performed compression tests at room temperature and at elevated temperatures (800 °C up to 1400 °C) at a strain rate of 10⁻³ s⁻¹ to evaluate yield strength, ultimate strength, ductility, and work hardening/softening behavior, and analyzed the contributions from solution strengthening (including estimated shear moduli and lattice distortion effects).
paper_reported: All as-cast alloys form a single-phase, disordered BCC solid solution; dendritic microstructures with compositional segregation (e.g. Ta- and Mo-rich dendrites) were observed.

Elemental additions and subtractions affect mechanical properties: for example, Mo boosts room-temperature yield strength but reduces ductility, while Nb improves ductility and sustains strength at elevated temperatures; high melting-point elements help maintain strength at high temperature.

The high yield strengths are primarily attributed to solid solution strengthening from modulus and atomic size mismatches (with a noted ~30% overestimation by the rule-of-mixtures), and the paper highlights the need for further modifications (e.g. composition changes or anti-oxidation coatings) for high-temperature applications in air.
paper_proposed: Future work should address further compositional modifications and/or the application of anti-oxidation coatings to enhance oxidation resistance in air at elevated temperatures.

Additional research is suggested to optimize the balance between yield strength, ductility, and oxidation resistance – for instance by adjusting Nb content to improve ductility and investigating the mechanisms underlying the reduced effective shear modulus.

hypotheses.hypothesis: A minor compositional modification by partially substituting one element (e.g. ~2 at.% Al replacing Ti) in equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr will improve its oxygen resistance through the in situ formation of a protective, slow-growing alumina (Al2O3) scale while preserving the useful room‐ and high‐temperature mechanical performance.
hypotheses.material_initial_state: Equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr produced by vacuum-arc melting that exhibits 8–16% room-temperature tensile ductility and acceptable high-temperature yield strength but poor oxidation resistance in air.
hypotheses.intervention: Introduce a small (approximately 2 atomic percent) addition of aluminum by partially replacing Ti in the alloy composition, resulting in a modified alloy composition such as HfNbTaTi_0.9Al_0.1Zr (approximately equiatomic with a minor Al addition).
hypotheses.conditions: Tested in air at 800 °C for a 5-hour exposure under strain rates of 10^−4–10^−2 s^−1; mechanical performance measured both at room temperature and elevated temperature (≈1000 °C).
hypotheses.structural_mediator: In situ formation of a continuous, adherent Al2O3 oxide layer on the surface.
hypotheses.mechanism: Aluminum, having a high affinity for oxygen, is expected to preferentially oxidize to form a dense and slow-growing alumina scale. Alumina is known for its excellent stability and low oxygen permeability. This external scale would act as a barrier to oxygen ingress during exposure at high temperature, reducing the oxidation (and pesting) of the underlying HfNbTaTiZr alloy. Since only a small fraction is added, the bulk solid solution structure (BCC) is preserved and the mechanical performance, directed by solid solution strengthening (as discussed in PMC7514121 sections 4.2 and 5), remains largely intact.
hypotheses.predicted_outcome: Improved high-temperature oxidation resistance with a significant reduction in oxygen penetration and pesting, while maintaining room-temperature ductility (≈8–16%) and high-temperature yield strength within the previously reported range. The effect size is expected to be substantial in oxidation resistance, though exact quantitative improvement is uncertain.
hypotheses.baseline: Untreated equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr exhibits inadequate oxygen resistance (experiencing pesting) in air at elevated temperatures.
hypotheses.boundary: The intervention is limited to a minor compositional change (<5 at.% Al) to avoid significant alteration of solid solution strengthening and ductility; tests are valid for air exposure up to 800 °C for durations near 5 hours at low strain rates.
hypotheses.uncertainty: The optimum level of Al addition is not precisely known; excessive Al could form brittle intermetallic phases or degrade ductility. Quantitative improvements in oxidation resistance are estimated qualitatively.

paper_did: Designed and prepared two novel Nb‐silicide based alloys (MG5: Nb1.45Si2.7Ti2.25Al3.25Hf0.35 and MG6: Nb1.35Si2.3Ti2.3Al3.7Hf0.35) using the NICE alloy design methodology.

Fabricated the alloys by arc‐melting into cast buttons, followed by heat treatments at 800 °C and 1200 °C and subsequent isothermal oxidation experiments (typically 100 hours long) at 800 °C and 1200 °C.

Characterized the microstructures and phase distributions using XRD, SEM, and EDS, documenting the formation of composite silicide grains, tri‐aluminides, Ti5Si4, TiSi, TiAl and changes in Nb/Ti ratios.
Demonstrated that the designed alloys formed a continuous, self‐healing α‐Al2O3 scale at high temperatures and analyzed defects such as cracking and incipient melting in specific phases.
paper_reported: The alloys met design criteria such as avoidance of pest oxidation and formation of a protective α‐Al2O3 scale, with each alloy displaying distinct microstructural features (e.g., the composite nature of silicide grains and variations in chemical homogeneity).
Detailed phase analyses revealed the presence of hexagonal γNb5Si3 as well as secondary phases (tri‐aluminides, Ti5Si4, TiSi, and TiAl) that influence oxidation behavior.

The oxidation behavior – including self‐healing ability of the oxide scale and mechanisms such as selective outward Al diffusion and the role of intermetallic interfaces – was elucidated, along with observations of cracking and incipient melting under certain conditions.
paper_proposed: Future work was suggested to improve coating systems for Nb‐silicide based alloys, including the exploration of layered or multi‐material bond coat approaches.

There were proposals to optimize chemical homogeneity and further refine the compositional maps for achieving more reliable formation of continuous, self‐healing alumina scales via controlled alloy design.

Distinct Sn‑rich areas developed beneath the oxide scales with varying continuity and thickness, and oxygen contamination within the substrate occurred primarily via Nb solid solution regions.

The study correlated oxidation improvements with changes in alloy parameters (like VEC and δ), and discussed the role of intermetallic phase stability (e.g., Nb3Sn) and the synergy of Sn with Al (and/or Cr) as key to achieving better high‑temperature oxidation performance.
paper_proposed: Exploring the optimum concentration of Sn needed to suppress pest oxidation and control scale spallation, and determining whether the stability of Nb3Sn is crucial for oxidation resistance.

Investigating the role of other elements (e.g., Al, Cr) in forming synergistic intermetallic compounds and modifying oxidation behavior, particularly in relation to oxide scale adhesion and oxygen contamination.

Assessing open questions such as why scale adherence is poor at higher temperatures in Sn‑containing alloys and whether combining Sn with other alloying additions can further enhance oxidation resistance.

paper_did: Synthesized three Nb‐based refractory complex concentrated alloys (TT5, TT6, TT7) via arc melting followed by a 100‐h heat treatment at 1500 °C.

Characterized the alloys’ microstructures (using XRD and EPMA) to identify phase constituents such as bcc Nb solid solution (Nbss), T2 and D88 silicides, as well as Nb3Sn and Nb3Si, and measured macrosegregation of elements (B, Si, Ti).
Measured key properties including density (<7 g/cm³), hardness (Vickers microhardness), and oxidation behavior (weight gain, scale spallation) during isothermal oxidation tests at 800 and 1200 °C.
paper_reported: TT6 exhibited the highest specific strength and superior oxidation performance compared to TT5 and TT7.
Distinct phase formation was observed: TT5 and TT7 contained a stable Nbss along with T2 and D88 silicides, while TT6 formed A15‐Nb3Sn together with T2 and D88 silicides.

Oxidation testing showed that although none of the B‐containing alloys pest at 800 °C, scale spallation occurred on TT5 (and on some B‐free references) especially at 1200 °C, with subtle effects of alloying additions (Hf, Sn, Ta) on macrosegregation and oxidation behavior.
paper_proposed: Further exploration of the synergistic effects of B with Sn or Hf on macrosegregation of Si and Ti to refine oxidation and microstructural control.
Application and fine‐tuning of the NICE alloy design methodology to further optimize compositions and property balances in refractory metallic UHTMs.
Investigation of parameter correlations and processing‐induced microstructural modifications to improve oxidation resistance while preserving mechanical performance.

paper_did: Synthesized and processed three Nb‐based refractory complex concentrated alloys (TT5, TT6, and TT7) with nominal compositions Nb–Ti–Cr–Al–B–Si–X (X = Ta, Sn, or Hf) by arc melting in argon and subsequent heat treatment at 1500 °C for 100 hours.

Characterized the alloys’ densities (all below 7 g/cm³), macrosegregation of key solutes (B, Ti, Si, etc.), phase composition (e.g., bcc Nbss, T2 and D88 silicides, and in one case Nb3Sn/Nb3Si), and microstructural features using XRD and EPMA.

paper_reported: The addition of Hf, Sn, or Ta influenced macrosegregation – reducing the segregation of B, Ti, and Si – and led to different phase equilibria across the alloys (with TT5 and TT7 stabilizing Nbss, T2 and D88, and TT6 yielding Nb3Sn along with T2 and D88).

TT6 exhibited the highest specific strength (both as cast and after heat treatment) along with the best hardness retention and favorable oxidation behavior (minimal mass gain and scale spallation, especially at 1200 °C).

The study demonstrated that alloying strategies guided by the NICE methodology can correlate phase parameters (δ, Δχ, VEC, etc.) with microstructural evolution and oxidation resistance, while also highlighting the need to better understand solute synergy (e.g., B with Sn or Hf) as a future research direction.
paper_proposed: Further investigations to understand the effects of alloying element synergies—especially how B interacts in combination with Sn or Hf—to control macrosegregation and oxidation behavior.

Refinements of the NICE alloy design guidelines to optimize phase balance and performance in metallic ultra-high-temperature materials, including more detailed analysis of oxidation responses and microstructural architecture.

paper_did: Synthesized three Nb‐based refractory complex concentrated alloys (TT5, TT6, TT7) with nominal compositions Nb‐24Ti‐18Si‐5Al‐5B‐5Cr‐6Ta, Nb‐24Ti‐18Si‐4Al‐6B‐5Cr‐4Sn, and Nb‐24Ti‐17Si‐5Al‐6B‐5Cr‐5Hf via arc melting followed by a 100‐hour heat treatment at 1500 °C.

Characterized the alloys’ microstructures, macrosegregation (of B, Si, Ti), phase constituents (including bcc Nbss, T2, D88 silicides, Nb3Si, Nb3Sn), densities, and hardness using XRD, EPMA, and Vickers hardness methods; and analyzed the effects of specific alloying additions (Hf, Sn, Ta) on these properties.

Conducted isothermal oxidation experiments at 800 and 1200 °C (up to 100 hours), evaluating mass changes, oxide scale spallation, and relating oxidation behavior to phase composition and alloy parameters (VEC, δ, Δχ) in line with the NICE (Niobium Intermetallic Composite Elaboration) design methodology.

Distinct microstructural features were identified: for example, TT5 contained Nbss, T2 and D88 silicides, Nb3Si and a Cr–Ti‐rich phase, while TT6 showed Nb3Sn along with T2 and D88, and TT7 exhibited a lower volumetric fraction of Nbss; the addition of Hf, Sn, or Ta influenced phase stability and macrosegregation patterns.

Oxidation tests revealed that none of the B‐containing alloys suffered pest oxidation at 800 °C, yet differences emerged at 1200 °C (with TT5 experiencing scale spallation), and trends in oxidation kinetics were consistent with correlations based on alloy parameters as per NICE.

paper_did: Developed three Nb‐based refractory complex concentrated alloys (TT5, TT6, and TT7) with different minor alloying additions (Ta, Sn, or Hf) on a B‐containing RM(Nb)IC/RCCA base.

Processed the alloys by arc melting (repeated remelting to ensure homogeneity) followed by a long heat treatment at 1500 °C for 100 hours, and measured density, macrosegregation, and microstructural phase distributions using XRD and electron probe analyses.

Characterized the materials’ mechanical (hardness) and oxidation properties through isothermal oxidation tests at 800 °C and 1200 °C (up to 100 hours) and correlated oxidation behavior with macrosegregation of key solutes (B, Si, and Ti).
paper_reported: TT6 exhibited the highest specific strength (in both as‐cast and heat‐treated conditions) with all alloys having densities below 7 g/cm³.

Distinct phase assemblages were identified – including the Nb-based solid solution (Nbss), the tetragonal T2 silicide, the hexagonal D88 silicide, and additional compounds such as Nb3Si (and Nb3Sn in TT6) – with compositional variations (e.g., in Si/B ratios) that correlated with the observed macrosegregation trends.

Oxidation behavior varied among the alloys: while none of the B‐containing alloys suffered pesting at 800 °C, scale spallation was noted (e.g., in TT5 at both 800 °C and 1200 °C) whereas the alloys TT6 and TT7 showed better oxide scale adherence; the paper also discussed how the synergy of B with Ta, Sn, or Hf affected segregation and, by extension, oxidation performance.
paper_proposed: Further exploration of the correlations between macrosegregation (MACB, MACSi, MACTi) and thermodynamic parameters to understand the solute‐partitioning behavior in these complex alloys.

Investigation of the synergistic effects of B with various alloying elements (Ta, Sn, and Hf) with respect to optimizing microstructural homogeneity and oxidation resistance, potentially guiding future alloy design via the NICE methodology.

This improves the adhesion and continuity of the protective oxide layer. Thermodynamic guidance ensures that the Y addition is low enough to avoid formation of brittle Y‐rich phases that would otherwise compromise mechanical properties.

paper_did: Designed two Nb‐silicide-based alloys (JZ4 and JZ5) using the NICE methodology, with careful control over alloying elements (including Ge, Sn, Ti, Mo, W, Al, Cr, Hf, and Si) and processed them via arc melting and a 1500 °C/100 h heat treatment.

Conducted extensive microstructural characterization (SEM, EDS, XRD) to identify phases (e.g., βNb5Si3, αNb5Si3, A15-Nb3X, TM5Sn2X, C14‐Cr2Nb Laves phase, and (Nb,W) solid solution) and measured densities, macrosegregation of Si, and hardness.

Tested isothermal oxidation performance at 800 °C and 1200 °C for 100 h (using TG analysis) and compared the weight gains and oxidation kinetics with other refractory metal alloys, while also calculating creep rates under conditions of 1200 °C and 170 MPa.
paper_reported: Both alloys exhibited complex, multiphase microstructures with identified silicide (Nb5Si3 in α and β forms) and intermetallic phases; the heat treatment modified phase distributions by forming a small fraction of a W-rich (Nb,W) solid solution and reducing macrosegregation.

Oxidation tests showed parabolic behavior at both 800 °C and 1200 °C, with low weight gains (e.g., ~0.82 mg/cm² and ~0.57 mg/cm² at 800 °C; 13.43 mg/cm² for JZ4 and 8.43 mg/cm² for JZ5 at 1200 °C) without pest oxidation or scale spallation.

The experimental results agreed well with the NICE alloy design predictions and comparisons were made with Ta-containing alloys, underscoring the potential for further alloy refinement to meet creep, toughness, and oxidation targets.
paper_proposed: The paper concludes by recommending further research into alloy modifications to balance high‐temperature oxidation resistance with creep and toughness goals, suggesting that exploring additional compositional adjustments (e.g., different combinations of alloying additions) and processing strategies might be necessary.

paper_did: Studied the Al-25.5Nb-6Cr-0.5Hf (at %) alloy in both cast and heat‐treated (1400 °C) conditions.
Conducted 100‐hour isothermal oxidation tests in air at temperatures of 800, 1200, and 1300 °C.
Characterized the microstructure, identifying primary phases such as DO22–NbAl3 and C14–NbCr2 Laves phase, along with eutectic regions and minor phases like HfO2.

Examined the oxidation products and scale formation, noting that at 800 °C both external and internal oxidation occur (with oxides like AlNbO4, CrNbAlO4, and α–Al2O3) while at 1200 and 1300 °C a two‐layer external scale forms (outer layer of (Al,Cr)NbO4 mixed with α–Al2O3 and an inner continuous α–Al2O3 layer).
Utilized parameter maps (δ, Δχ, VEC) to correlate composition with oxidation behavior and to guide the design of candidate bond coat alloys for environmentally resistant coatings.
paper_reported: At 800 °C, the alloy exhibited both external and deeper internal oxidation with formation of compounds including AlNbO4, CrNbAlO4, and α–Al2O3.
At 1200 and 1300 °C, only external oxidation occurred, resulting in a layered oxide scale—an outer mixed (Al,Cr)NbO4/α–Al2O3 layer and an inner continuous α–Al2O3 layer.
Hf functions as a reactive element that improves the adhesion of the oxide scale.
The microstructure (mainly NbAl3 and NbCr2) and oxidation behavior compare favorably with alumina‐forming intermetallic systems as mapped by δ, Δχ, and VEC parameters.
paper_proposed: Investigate whether alloys containing DO22–NbAl3 and C14–NbCr2 phases can maintain oxidation resistance (i.e., avoid pesting) and form continuous protective alumina scales.
Explore the potential for these alloys to serve as bond coat candidates in environmentally resistant coating systems for Nb–silicide based substrates.
Examine microstructural transitions (e.g., formation of Zone A microstructures) and optimize alloying additions (e.g., Cr and Hf) to achieve the desired oxidation behavior and phase stability.

hypotheses.hypothesis: A pack aluminiding treatment on the surface of equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr will form an Al-enriched outer layer that, upon high-temperature exposure, converts to a continuous, adherent α-Al2O3 scale, thereby dramatically improving oxygen resistance while retaining the bulk mechanical properties.
hypotheses.material_initial_state: Cast equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr with its as-cast microstructure and measured ductility and high‐temperature yield strength.
hypotheses.intervention: Apply a pack cementation aluminiding treatment to introduce an Al-rich surface layer (e.g., via a controlled diffusion process in an Al-containing powder mixture) without altering the bulk composition.
hypotheses.conditions: Oxidation testing in air at 800–1000 °C for durations from 5 to 100 h; mechanical testing unchanged at room temperature and 1000 °C under strain rates of 10^(-4)–10^(-2) s^(-1).
hypotheses.structural_mediator: Formation of an externally continuous α-Al2O3 scale on the aluminized surface.
hypotheses.mechanism: The introduced aluminum diffuses to the surface at high temperature and preferentially oxidizes to form a dense, slow-growing alumina layer. This scale acts as an effective barrier to oxygen diffusion (as predicted by Wagner’s oxidation theory and demonstrated in Al-rich intermetallic systems [PMC6719109::web::abstracts]), leveraging the high thermodynamic stability of alumina over the native oxides of Hf, Nb, Ta, Ti, and Zr.
hypotheses.predicted_outcome: Significantly reduced oxidation rate and prevention of pesting (oxygen-induced embrittlement) relative to untreated material, with a maintained ductility of 8–16% at RT and yield strength of ~163–530 MPa at 1000 °C. The improvement is expected to be moderate to large, though precise gain size is uncertain.
hypotheses.baseline: Untreated equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr showing inadequate oxygen resistance under the same conditions.
hypotheses.boundary: Applicable for high-temperature exposures in air in the 800–1000 °C range and exposure durations up to 100 h; the surface treatment depth should be limited so as not to affect the bulk mechanical performance.
hypotheses.uncertainty: Quantitative improvement in oxidation kinetics (e.g., parabolic rate constants) is uncertain without experimental data; scale adhesion and long-term cyclic oxidation resistance need confirmation.

hypotheses.builds_on: The finding from the paper that reactive element additions (e.g., Hf in Al-based alloys) improve scale adhesion and promote formation of alumina scales, extended here by applying a surface modification to introduce Al selectively.
hypotheses.what_is_new: This hypothesis proposes a surface-specific modification (pack aluminiding) to improve oxidation resistance of equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr without altering its bulk composition, a strategy not reported in the prior work which focused on bulk alloy composition and phase design.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Localized laser surface alloying with chromium on cast equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr will produce a Cr-enriched surface layer that forms a protective Cr2O3 scale during high-temperature exposure, thus enhancing oxygen resistance while leaving the core properties intact.
hypotheses.material_initial_state: Cast equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr with homogeneous elemental distribution and established mechanical performance.
hypotheses.intervention: Apply a rapid laser surface alloying process to melt a thin surface layer in the presence of a pre-deposited Cr paste, resulting in a Cr-enriched surface zone.
hypotheses.conditions: High-temperature exposure in air at 800–1000 °C and similar mechanical testing (RT tensile ductility 8–16%, yield strength ~163–530 MPa at 1000 °C), with oxidation duration ranging from 5 to 50 h.
hypotheses.structural_mediator: Formation of a thin, continuous Cr2O3 layer on the alloy’s surface.
hypotheses.mechanism: Chromium has a more negative oxide formation enthalpy compared to several base elements and a smaller atomic radius (similar to the way Cr additions improve selective oxidation behavior in Nb-Al systems as noted in the paper [PMC6719109::web::015::2_alloy_selection]). The laser alloying results in a concentrated Cr surface that, upon high-temperature oxidation, preferentially forms Cr2O3. In dry air at moderate temperatures, Cr2O3 can provide an effective barrier to oxygen ingress, slowing further oxidation.
hypotheses.predicted_outcome: A reduction in oxidation rate at 800–1000 °C with improved oxygen resistance compared to the untreated alloy; mechanical properties remain largely unchanged because the modified layer is very thin relative to the specimen’s cross-section.
hypotheses.baseline: Oxygen resistance of untreated equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr, which demonstrates inadequate oxidation performance.
hypotheses.boundary: Effective in dry air environments at 800–1000 °C for oxidation exposures up to about 50 h; the laser-treated depth must remain shallow (a few tens of microns) to avoid altering bulk mechanical behavior.
hypotheses.uncertainty: The long-term stability of the Cr2O3 scale and its performance under cyclic oxidation or in humid atmospheres requires further validation. The quantitative improvement in oxidation resistance is not precisely predicted.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Aluminum ion implantation of the surface of cast equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr will create a metastable, Al-enriched near-surface region that, during subsequent high-temperature exposure, rapidly transforms into a self-healing, protective α-Al2O3 scale, thereby enhancing oxygen resistance without altering bulk performance.
hypotheses.material_initial_state: Cast equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr exhibiting its inherent microstructure and mechanical properties.
hypotheses.intervention: Conduct a controlled aluminum ion implantation process (with energy and dose tailored to achieve a ~1–3 μm implanted layer) to enrich only the top surface region with Al.
hypotheses.conditions: Post-implantation oxidation testing in air at 800–1000 °C for exposure times ranging from 5 to 50 h, with mechanical testing conducted to verify that bulk properties (8–16% RT tensile ductility and yield strength 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C) are preserved.
hypotheses.structural_mediator: A thin, self-healing α-Al2O3 scale that forms in situ from the Al-implanted layer.
hypotheses.mechanism: The ion implantation introduces Al atoms into the near-surface region without modifying the overall bulk composition. During high-temperature oxidation, the implanted Al segregates and reacts with oxygen to form a dense, adherent α-Al2O3 layer. The self-healing nature of alumina (due to its low oxygen diffusivity and high thermodynamic stability) impedes further oxygen penetration, as predicted by oxidation theory and analogous to reactive element effects observed in aluminide coatings [PMC6719109::web::016::2_alloy_selection].
hypotheses.predicted_outcome: A marked improvement in oxidation resistance evidenced by significantly lower oxidation weight gain and enhanced protection from pesting during exposure at 800–1000 °C, while the bulk mechanical properties remain unaffected due to the shallow modification depth.
hypotheses.baseline: The unchanged oxygen resistance and oxidation kinetics of untreated equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr.

paper_did: It investigated the microstructure and oxidation behavior of a Nb‐silicide–based alloy with nominal composition Al–25.5Nb–6Cr–0.5Hf in both cast and heat‐treated (1400 °C) conditions.
It performed isothermal oxidation experiments in air for 100 hours at three temperatures (800 °C, 1200 °C, and 1300 °C) to study external versus internal oxidation and scale formation.

It characterized the stable phases (primarily NbAl3 and C14–NbCr2, with minor (Cr,Al,Nb) solid solution and HfO2) and correlated the oxidation processes (e.g., formation of AlNbO4, CrNbAlO4, layered scales with continuous α–Al2O3) with processing and composition.
It employed design maps based on parameters (δ, Δχ, and VEC) and discussed the role of reactive element additions (notably Hf) in enhancing oxide adhesion.
paper_reported: At 800 °C the alloy resisted catastrophic pest oxidation but showed both external and internal oxidation—with external scales containing AlNbO4, CrNbAlO4, and α–Al2O3 and internal oxidation along NbAl3/Laves phase boundaries.

At 1200 °C and 1300 °C only external oxidation occurred, forming a two‐layer scale (outer (Al,Cr)NbO4 mixed with α–Al2O3 and an inner continuous α–Al2O3 layer), while no Nb2Al was observed below the interface.
Hf in the alloy acted as a reactive element by forming HfO2 that enhanced oxide scale adhesion, and the study connected these findings with established alloy design criteria using δ, Δχ, and VEC.
paper_proposed: To address challenges in achieving an oxidation‐resistant, alumina‐forming coating system for Nb–silicide–based alloys, the paper raised questions about the formation of continuous α–Al2O3 scales, the possibility of avoiding pest oxidation even at lower temperatures than 1200 °C, and the compatibility of such alloys with different coating alloys.
Future work was suggested to explore optimized compositions and microstructures—such as achieving a layered or Zone A microstructure—that enhance selective oxidation and scale adherence.

paper_did: Prepared cast Ti-45Al-8.5Nb alloy specimens (10 × 10 × 5 mm³) via cutting, grinding, and polishing.
Applied a surface treatment by spraying a NaF‐containing aqueous solution (0.15 mol/L), followed by washing and drying.

Conducted isothermal oxidation experiments at 1000 °C on both pristine and artificially defected (scratched) specimens, including a two‐step process (initial oxidation then re‐treatment of cracked surfaces with NaF and subsequent oxidation).
Characterized the microstructure, phase composition, and oxide scale evolution using SEM, EDS, XRD, TEM, and contact angle measurements; and measured oxidation kinetics via mass gain analysis.
paper_reported: The fluorine treatment significantly reduced oxidation weight gain (from 6.03 mg/cm² for the bare alloy to 0.81 mg/cm² for the fluorine‐treated alloy).
Fluorine promoted the formation of a dense and continuous Al₂O₃ film that provided enhanced adhesion and improved oxidation resistance.
In specimens with artificially induced microcracks, rapid diffusion led initially to TiO₂ formation, whereas prolonged oxidation resulted in a continuous Al₂O₃ film beneath the oxide scale.
The protective mechanism was attributed to selective oxidation facilitated by the vaporization of metal fluorides (e.g., Al‐fluoride) and the consequent formation of protective oxide layers.
paper_proposed: The study suggests that the fluorine treatment strategy could be applied as a repair method for protective oxide films on engineering components such as blades and turbine disks.
It hints at further exploration of surface modification via fluorine incorporation for improved high‐temperature oxidation behavior in γ-TiAl alloys.

paper_did: Prepared cast Ti‐45Al‐8.5Nb alloy specimens by vacuum induction melting, cutting and mechanical polishing.
Applied a surface treatment by spraying a NaF‐containing aqueous solution (0.15 mol/L) onto the specimens.
Performed isothermal oxidation experiments at 1000 °C, including tests on specimens with artificial microcracks (introduced by scratching) and subsequent re‐treatment with the F‐solution.
Characterized the oxidized and fluorine‐treated samples using SEM, EDS, XRD, and TEM.
Measured oxidation kinetics (weight gain) and wetting behavior (contact angle) to evaluate the effectiveness of the fluorine treatment.
paper_reported: Fluorine treatment dramatically improved oxidation resistance by reducing mass gain from 6.03 mg/cm² (bare alloy) to 0.81 mg/cm² (fluorine‐treated), associated with the formation of a protective oxide scale.
The fluorine effect promoted the formation of a continuous, dense Al₂O₃ film that enhanced the adhesion of the oxide scale to the substrate.
In specimens with artificial defects, microcracks provided diffusion paths that initially led to rapid TiO₂ growth; with longer oxidation, a continuous Al₂O₃ film evolved underneath the oxide scale.

XRD and TEM analyses confirmed the presence of oxide phases (TiO₂, Al₂O₃) as well as intermetallic phases (γ‐TiAl, α₂‐Ti₃Al) and revealed compositional gradients (Al₂O₃‐rich top layer, Al‐depleted subsurface, Nb‐rich interface).
paper_proposed: The study suggests that the fluorine treatment could be further employed for repairing the protective oxide films on engineering components such as turbine blades and disks made from γ‐TiAl alloys.
It hints at extending the surface‐modification approach for in‐situ repair of oxidation‐damaged surfaces in practical, large‐scale applications.

paper_did: Fabricated cast Ti‐45Al‐8.5Nb alloy specimens via vacuum induction melting, then prepared them by cutting, grinding, and polishing.
Applied a surface treatment by spraying a NaF‐containing aqueous solution (0.15 mol/L) onto the alloy specimens.
Conducted isothermal oxidation experiments at 1000 °C on both pristine and fluorine–treated specimens, including tests on specimens with artificial microcracks.
Characterized the oxidized samples using SEM, EDS, XRD, TEM, and contact angle measurements to analyze the microstructure, chemical composition, and oxidation kinetics.
paper_reported: Fluorine treatment promoted the formation of a continuous, protective Al₂O₃ film that reduced oxidation-induced mass gain from 6.03 mg/cm² (bare alloys) to 0.81 mg/cm² (fluorine-treated alloys).

Artificial microcracks served as rapid diffusion pathways for Ti and O, leading initially to quick TiO₂ growth, while prolonged oxidation resulted in a fine, adherent Al₂O₃ film beneath the outer oxide scale.
A hierarchical oxide structure was observed—with an Al₂O₃-rich top layer, an Al-depleted subsurface, and a Nb-rich layer—that enhanced the adhesion of the oxide scale to the substrate.
paper_proposed: The study proposed that the fluorine treatment strategy could be used as an approach for repairing damaged protective oxide films (for instance, on turbine blades and disks), leveraging the in‐situ reformation of a continuous Al₂O₃ layer.

hypotheses.hypothesis: HF Vapor Pretreatment to Form Protective HfO2/ZrO2 Scale
hypotheses.material_initial_state: Cast equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr with homogeneous elemental distribution and a native, nonprotective oxide film.
hypotheses.intervention: Expose the alloy to a controlled HF vapor atmosphere at an intermediate temperature (around 300 °C) for approximately 10 minutes.
hypotheses.conditions: After HF vapor pretreatment, the specimens will be oxidized in air at 800 °C for 5 hours under tensile loading (strain rates of 10⁻⁴–10⁻² s⁻¹) and subsequently characterized by tensile tests at room temperature and 800 °C.
hypotheses.structural_mediator: A thin, modified surface layer in which Hf and Zr are converted transiently to fluoride species (e.g. HfF₄ and ZrF₄) that decompose during oxidation into a dense, adherent HfO₂/ZrO₂ composite scale.
hypotheses.mechanism: HF vapor reacts with surface Hf and Zr to form transient fluoride precursors. During subsequent high-temperature oxidation, these fluorides decompose into HfO₂ and ZrO₂. These oxides are known for their low oxygen diffusivity and high thermodynamic stability, thereby creating an effective oxygen diffusion barrier while leaving the bulk microstructure and mechanical performance largely unaltered.
hypotheses.predicted_outcome: Treated specimens will develop a continuous, adherent HfO₂/ZrO₂-dominated oxide scale with a reduction in oxidation mass gain by an estimated 40–60% relative to untreated specimens, while preserving ductility and yield strength.
hypotheses.baseline: Untreated equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr forms a porous or nonuniform oxide scale that permits rapid oxygen ingress and causes mechanical degradation at high temperature.
hypotheses.boundary: The HF vapor treatment is confined to the surface (a few tens of nanometers in depth) and is optimized for oxidation conditions of 800 °C and a 5-hour exposure under controlled tensile strain. The processing parameter (temperature, HF exposure duration) must be maintained to prevent excessive fluorination or bulk chemical alteration.
hypotheses.uncertainty: Uncertainty remains regarding the selectivity of HF vapor for Hf and Zr versus Ti, Nb, and Ta in a complex high-entropy system. Thermodynamic and kinetic details of fluoride formation in this specific alloy require further experimental validation.

The ultrathin ALD-deposited film remains adherent during high-temperature exposure, preventing oxygen ingress and subsequent pesting, without affecting bulk alloy properties due to its minimal thickness.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Surface Yttrium Modification via Immersion Treatment to Enhance Oxide Scale Adhesion

hypotheses.conditions: Following the Y-treatment, specimens will be oxidized in air at 800 °C for 5 hours under tensile loading (strain rates of 10⁻⁴–10⁻² s⁻¹) and subsequently evaluated through tensile tests at room temperature and 800 °C.
hypotheses.structural_mediator: A surface layer interspersed with finely dispersed Y₂O₃ particles that promote a strong metal-oxide interface during high-temperature oxidation.
hypotheses.mechanism: Yttrium is a reactive element that, when present at the oxide scale/substrate interface, improves scale adhesion by reducing spallation and modifying defect structures at the interface. The dispersed Y₂O₃ particles facilitate the formation of a more uniform and well-adherent oxide scale (likely a mixed oxide including HfO₂, Nb/Ta oxides, and residual TiO₂/ZrO₂), thereby reducing oxygen ingress and enhancing oxidation resistance without altering the beneficial bulk mechanical properties.

The process must be controlled to prevent excessive Y uptake that could alter bulk composition.
hypotheses.uncertainty: The main uncertainty lies in achieving a uniform and controlled Y₂O₃ dispersion at the surface and quantifying the precise improvement in oxide scale adhesion in this complex alloy system.

paper_did: Prepared AlCoCrFeNi high‐entropy alloy coatings by atmospheric plasma spraying using gas-atomized powders on Ni-based substrates.
Subjected the coatings to isothermal oxidation at 650 °C, 800 °C, 900 °C, and 1000 °C for various durations (20 h, 50 h, 100 h) in air.
Characterized the microstructural and phase evolution during oxidation using XRD, SEM, and EDS to observe oxide scale formation and internal phase transitions.
paper_reported: At lower temperatures (650 °C), almost no oxide formed on the coating surface, while at higher temperatures (800–900 °C and above) a laminated oxide scale developed, consisting of a mixed oxide surface layer and an underlying continuous Al2O3 sub-layer.

The oxidation process induced element redistribution leading to phase transitions within the coating – notably, transformation from a BCC/B2 structure into Al–Ni rich ordered B2 phases and Fe–Cr rich disordered A2 phases, with further BCC to FCC transformation linked to Al depletion.
The formation, continuity, and thickness of the oxide layers as well as the evolution of internal microstructure were strongly dependent on oxidation temperature and exposure time.
paper_proposed: Although no explicit future work experiments were detailed, the paper emphasizes the need for a more comprehensive understanding of high temperature oxidation and phase transformation in AlCoCrFeNi coatings, which hints at further investigation into controlling oxide scale construction and interfacial diffusion phenomena.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Minor aluminum addition to equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr will promote the in situ formation of a continuous, protective Al2O3 scale during high-temperature exposure, thereby improving its oxygen resistance while preserving its mechanical performance.
hypotheses.material_initial_state: Equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr, which in its untreated state shows inadequate oxygen resistance at high temperatures and maintains useful room‐temperature ductility and high‐temperature yield strength.
hypotheses.intervention: Introduce a small amount (e.g., 3–5 atomic %) of aluminum into the alloy composition.
hypotheses.conditions: High-temperature exposure in air between 800 °C and 1000 °C for durations up to 100 h; tensile loading conditions unchanged from current state to ensure mechanical performance is preserved.
hypotheses.structural_mediator: The formation of a laminated oxide structure with an outer, mixed oxide layer and an inner, dense Al2O3 sub-layer.
hypotheses.mechanism: The selective oxidation of the added Al at high temperature produces a continuous and slow-growing alumina (Al2O3) scale. This scale acts as an oxygen diffusion barrier, reducing further oxidation of the alloy matrix. The protective role of alumina in forming durable oxide scales is analogous to that observed in AlCoCrFeNi coatings where continuous Al2O3 layers were key to improved oxidation resistance (see PMC10856430::web::009 and PMC10856430::web::014).
hypotheses.predicted_outcome: A significant reduction in the oxidation rate relative to the untreated alloy, with improved oxygen resistance during high-temperature exposure while maintaining ductility and yield strength. Exact improvement is uncertain, but a reduction in oxidation kinetics on the order of those seen in protective alumina-forming systems is expected.
hypotheses.baseline: Performance of the untreated equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr, which suffers from rapid oxidation/pesting at high temperatures.
hypotheses.boundary: Intervention applies only to bulk composition modification up to a few atomic percent aluminum; exposure conditions are limited to air at 800–1000 °C for up to 100 h; mechanical loading not exceeding that used in current high-temperature tensile tests.
hypotheses.uncertainty: The precise impact on the phase stability and mechanical properties (ductility and yield strength) may vary; minimal Al addition is expected to avoid deleterious effects, but microstructural evolution warrants careful evaluation.

hypotheses.hypothesis: A controlled pre-oxidation heat treatment in a reduced oxygen partial pressure can form a thin, adherent, self-healing oxide scale on equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr that enhances its oxygen resistance during service.
hypotheses.material_initial_state: Equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr with a native, non-protective oxide formation tendency during high-temperature exposure.
hypotheses.intervention: Apply a post-casting, pre-service heat treatment in a controlled atmosphere with low oxygen partial pressure (e.g., a slightly oxidizing atmosphere or diluted air) at an intermediate temperature.
hypotheses.conditions: Anneal the alloy at about 700 °C for a short time (e.g., 1–5 h) in an atmosphere with controlled oxygen partial pressure (for example, 10–20% O2 balanced with inert gas), followed by subsequent exposures at 800–1000 °C in air for up to 100 h under similar tensile loading conditions as the untreated alloy.
hypotheses.structural_mediator: The formation of a uniform, adherent, and thin oxide layer (likely mixed oxides with significant contributions from HfO2 and possibly TiO2) that is continuous and acts as an oxygen barrier.
hypotheses.mechanism: The pre-oxidation treatment enables controlled surface oxidation in a regime where oxygen diffusivity is moderated. By establishing a thin and adherent oxide scale before severe oxidation can occur, subsequent high-temperature exposures in air lead only to minor thickening of this scale rather than catastrophic pesting. The pre-formed layer restricts further oxygen ingress, similar to how protective oxide scales function in high-entropy coatings (PMC10856430::web::004 and PMC10856430::web::007).
hypotheses.predicted_outcome: The pre-oxidized alloy will exhibit a much slower oxidation rate during subsequent high-temperature exposure compared to the untreated material, while maintaining its inherent ductility and yield strength. The scale is anticipated to slow the oxidation kinetics significantly, though the exact quantitative improvement is uncertain.
hypotheses.baseline: The oxidation behavior and mechanical performance of the untreated equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr when exposed directly to high-temperature air.
hypotheses.boundary: The intervention is confined to a post-casting heat treatment step at approximately 700 °C in a controlled low-O2 atmosphere; service conditions remain in air at between 800 °C and 1000 °C up to 100 h with standard tensile loadings.
hypotheses.uncertainty: The exact composition and adherence quality of the pre-formed oxide scale may vary; if the scale is not sufficiently protective or if it spalls during mechanical loading, the benefits could be reduced.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Introducing a trace amount of yttrium into equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr will improve the adherence and slow the growth of the native oxide scale during high-temperature exposures, thereby enhancing its oxygen resistance while retaining mechanical integrity.

hypotheses.mechanism: Reactive element effects: Yttrium atoms segregate to the metal/oxide interface, leading to fewer defects and grain boundary channels in the oxide layer. paper_did: Prepared AlCoCrFeNi high‐entropy coatings by atmospheric plasma spraying (APS) using gas‐atomized, equiatomic powders on Ni‐based substrates.
Performed controlled isothermal oxidation experiments at temperatures ranging from 650 °C to 1000 °C for different durations (20 h, 50 h, 100 h, and one case of 200 h) under static air conditions.

Characterized the coatings using X-ray diffraction (XRD), scanning electron microscopy (SEM), and energy dispersive spectroscopy (EDS) to determine phase composition, microstructural features (surface and cross-sectional morphology), and elemental diffusion.

Tracked the evolution of oxide scales – from initial mixed oxide particle formation to the establishment of a continuous, laminated oxide layer (mixed oxides on top and an Al2O3-rich layer underneath) – and documented concomitant phase transformations (e.g., BCC/B2 to Al–Ni­-rich ordered B2 and Fe–Cr-rich disordered A2, with eventual BCC–FCC transition) during oxidation.
paper_reported: At lower oxidation temperatures (650 °C), very limited oxidation was observed with almost no oxide on the surface, though some oxides appeared in the lamellar gaps.
At 800 °C, discontinuous and scattered oxide particles (predominantly Al2O3 and spinel oxides) formed on the surface, with an incipient aluminum‐poor layer developing beneath.

At higher temperatures (900 °C and 1000 °C), a continuous dense oxide layer developed – initially exhibiting needle-like θ-Al2O3 that transformed to α-Al2O3 – along with pronounced elemental diffusion (especially depletion of Al) that triggered phase transitions (e.g., from BCC/B2 to FCC and evolution of A2 and B2 phases).

The study demonstrated that the formation of a protective, continuous oxide scale (particularly with Al2O3 formation) is closely linked to the oxidation kinetics and internal diffusion processes in the coating.
paper_proposed: The work implicitly points toward the need for further investigations that optimize processing parameters and compositional tweaks in high-entropy coatings to improve oxidation resistance and control phase transformations.

It suggests that understanding and controlling the evolution (continuity, thickness, and layering) of the oxide scale and the associated internal diffusion could be pivotal for tailoring coating performance for high‐temperature applications (e.g., as protective coatings in aero-engines).

paper_did: Deposited multilayered CrAlN/Al2O3 solar selective absorber coatings using a combination of HiPIMS, RF, and DC magnetron sputtering onto substrates (SS316, Inconel 625, and silicon), applying a simultaneous negative bias (–100 V) during deposition to densify the films.

Performed short‐term (2 h at 600, 700, and 800 °C) and long‐term (200 h at 600 °C) thermal annealing treatments in air and compared the thermal stability and oxidation resistance of the coatings with those of an unbiased stack and a commercial Pyromark paint reference.

Characterized the coatings extensively using GIXRD, SEM, TEM, EDX, Raman, and optical reflectance measurements to evaluate microstructure, chemical composition, phase transformations, and optical performance (solar absorptance and thermal emittance).
paper_reported: Bias-assisted coatings exhibited a denser, less columnar microstructure relative to films grown without bias, which translated into improved thermal stability and delayed degradation (e.g., later onset of Cr2N formation) at high temperatures.

The coatings maintained high solar absorptance (~93–95%) and low thermal emittance (≈15–18%) after thermal treatments, leading to enhanced solar-to-mechanical energy conversion efficiencies compared to commercial Pyromark paint.

The performance and oxidation behaviour were found to depend on substrate type, with SS316 generally outperforming Inconel 625, and the additional ion bombardment during deposition was identified as a key factor for the improved durability.
paper_proposed: Future work proposed comparisons between bias‐assisted and unbiased coating stacks under various thermal exposure conditions, including extended annealing times, to further validate and optimize the coating performance.

paper_did: Deposited a multilayer CrAlN/Al2O3 solar selective absorber coating using a combination of HiPIMS, RF, and DC magnetron sputtering with a simultaneous negative bias (–100 V) on substrates (SS316, Inconel 625, and silicon).

Varied the chemical composition across layers (from a Cr-rich, substoichiometric CrAlN layer serving as an IR reflector/absorber to layers with increasing Al content) and included an antireflective alumina top layer.

Subjected the coatings to thermal annealing treatments in air at 600, 700, and 800 °C for 2 hours, as well as a prolonged 200-hour annealing at 600 °C, to assess thermal stability and oxidation resistance.

Performed extensive characterization using XRD, SEM (including cross-sectional imaging), TEM with EDX mapping, Raman spectroscopy, ion beam analysis, and optical reflectance measurements to determine phase evolution, microstructure, stoichiometry, and optical properties.
paper_reported: Bias-assisted deposition produced denser, less columnar multilayer films that delayed the onset of detrimental phase transformations (e.g., delayed formation of Cr2N) compared to unbiased coatings.

The coatings maintained high solar absorptance (≈94–95%) and low thermal emittance (<20%) after high-temperature exposures, resulting in enhanced solar-to-mechanical energy conversion efficiency relative to commercial Pyromark paint.

Microstructural and chemical analyses confirmed that the graded composition in the multilayer stack and the densification achieved via negative bias contributed to improved oxidation resistance by impeding oxygen ingress and interdiffusion.

Optical performance trends and phase evolution with increasing annealing temperature were correlated, showing that bias assistance fostered better thermal stability and resistance to high-temperature degradation.
paper_proposed: Future studies were indicated to include direct comparisons between biased and unbiased stacks under similar thermal conditions, extended thermal cycling, and more in‐depth evaluations of the oxidation and interdiffusion mechanisms.

There is an implication to further optimize the multilayer design and investigate substrate effects to achieve coatings with even higher durability and efficiency for high-temperature solar absorber applications.
